One-sentence verdict: this line of work is not "swapping parts"; it is repairing, maintaining or installing computers, word processing systems, automated teller machines (ATMs) and office electronic equipment such as copiers and fax machines, restoring equipment to a usable state. O*NET defines the occupation as "repair, maintain, or install computers, word processing systems, automated teller machines, and electronic office machines, such as duplicating and fax machines," and its tasks rank "travel to customers' stores or offices to repair equipment or provide emergency repair service" and "reassemble machines after making repairs or replacing parts" as the top two; this page follows the exact occupational scope of O*NET-SOC 49-2011.00.

Signals for exploring further: you are willing to order the tests by symptom, willing to work with your hands on precision parts, and you accept that "explaining clearly + writing complete records" is part of the job. O*NET work context shows 94% have telephone conversations every day, 87% use email every day (11% never), 76% have face-to-face discussions every day (11% never), 71% use their hands to handle objects and tools continuously or almost continuously (23% less than half the time), 63% consider dealing with external customers or the public extremely important (13% very important), 64% face strict deadlines every day (12% more than once a week), 63% make decisions every day that affect others or financial resources or the organization's reputation (15% never), 57% consider repetitive tasks extremely important (23% not at all important), 40% stand continuously or almost continuously (26% more than half the time), 35% consider being very exact or highly accurate extremely important, 33% are in an enclosed vehicle or operating enclosed equipment every day (23% never), 28% are exposed to contaminants every day (16% never), 22% are exposed every day to minor burns and cuts and bites or stings (32% never), 18% are exposed to hazardous conditions every day (37% never), 82% have a regular fixed schedule, and 94% never come into contact with whole body vibration.

Conditions for pausing before heavy investment: you have not yet completed one full loop of "taking the work order and communicating on site — disassembly, inspection and testing — deciding whether the fault is mechanical or electrical — replacing parts — retesting and calibration — customer confirmation and work order filing," and you have not verified your employer's mandatory requirements for live electrical work, isolation and prevention of unexpected re-energization, access to and confidentiality of data on customer equipment, and warranty and asset responsibility. This occupation's preparation level is Job Zone 1-2 (little to some preparation), the page's education distribution is expressed as "usually requires a high school diploma or equivalent, some positions do not," and the SVP range is below 6.0; this page does not infer individual hiring probability from that.

Education, on-the-job training, professional certifications, licenses and job authorization must be verified separately: O*NET lists this occupation as Job Zone 1-2 (little to some preparation), the page's education distribution is expressed as "usually requires a high school diploma or equivalent, some positions do not," related experience ranges from little to a few months up to a year, on-the-job training ranges from a few days to a year, and the SVP range is below 6.0; the page also lists 8 national certifications (such as CompTIA A+ Certification, Certified Electronics Technician - Journeyman-Level - Computer, Certified Network Computer Technician, Computer Service Technician, Fiber Optics Technician, Wireless Communications, among others), but a certification is not equal to a degree, an employer appointment, manufacturer authorization or a live electrical work permit; live electrical work and isolation and prevention of unexpected re-energization, access to and confidentiality of personal information on customer equipment, and warranty and asset responsibility must be confirmed item by item according to the applicable jurisdiction and employer policies; this page describes tasks and boundaries based on O*NET and public sources, and does not present education or certifications as statutory qualifications.

In one sentence: this is an occupation in which "judging accurately, a steady hand, and explaining clearly" are all indispensable; whether the equipment is fixed in one visit, whether the customer understands, and whether the records support warranty and billing determine your reputation and income in this line. If you are willing to face customer sites and repetitive troubleshooting over the long term, it is worth serious consideration.

The work of Computer, Automated Teller, and Office Machine Repairers can be divided into three connected but distinct work areas. The first is on-site diagnosis and fault localization: travel to customers' stores or offices to repair equipment or provide emergency repair service; talk with customers to establish the details of the equipment problem; disassemble machines to inspect wires, gears, bearings and similar parts for wear or defects, using hand or power tools and measuring instruments; use oscilloscopes, signal generators, ammeters, voltmeters or specialized diagnostic software to test parts or circuits of faulty equipment to locate defects; and read blueprints, charts or schematics to determine equipment settings or adjustment parameters. The second is repair and parts replacement and retesting: use hand tools, power tools or soldering equipment to repair, adjust or replace electrical or mechanical parts; reassemble machines after making repairs or replacing parts; operate machines to test the function of parts or mechanisms; assemble equipment to specifications; align, adjust or calibrate equipment to specifications; calibrate test instruments; and clean, oil or adjust mechanical parts to maintain operating efficiency and prevent failures. The third is installation, configuration and customers and records: install and configure new equipment, including operating system software or peripherals; reinstall software programs or adjust existing software settings to fix equipment faults; update existing equipment, such as installing updated circuit boards or adding memory; test new systems to ensure they are in working order; maintain parts inventory and order other parts needed for repairs; explain equipment operation, maintenance or programming to customers; maintain equipment maintenance or repair records; and complete repair bills, shop records, time cards or expense reports.

Six recurring occupational judgments: whether isolation and prevention of unexpected re-energization are completed per procedure; whether symptoms and test results support the diagnostic conclusion; whether replacement and adjustment are traceable and can be retested; whether data on customer equipment is limited to the necessary scope; whether warranty and asset and work order responsibility stays within the scope of authority; and whether repair bills and inventory records match the actual actions.
Check one: are isolation and prevention of unexpected re-energization completed per procedure

Isolate the equipment per the applicable procedure before disassembling electrical parts and prevent unexpected re-energization; confirm the equipment and power and line status before starting work; do not treat diagnostic convenience as authorization for live work, and do not skip personal protective equipment and tool checks.
Check two: do the symptoms and test results support the diagnostic conclusion

Turn the customer's description of symptoms into testable hypotheses and rule them out item by item with results from an oscilloscope or multimeter or diagnostic software; distinguish mechanical faults from electrical faults and avoid replacing parts directly from experience; for faults that cannot be reproduced, write down the conditions and the limits of observation.
Check three: are replacement and adjustment traceable and retestable

Record the replaced part's model and source and serial number (where obtainable) and the condition of the original part; complete assembly and alignment and calibration to specifications and retest; write the test data into the work order so that warranty and billing and review have a basis.
Check four: is data on customer equipment limited to the necessary scope

Access customer data only within the lawful, clearly defined purpose and minimum necessary scope required by the repair; before backing up or resetting, verify the processing basis, customer notice and organizational authorization and record them. Written confirmation may serve as an editorial suggestion, but it cannot be said that the personal information protection law requires written consent for all repairs.
Check five: do warranty and asset and work order responsibilities stay within the scope of authority

Disassembly, parts replacement, program installation and service restoration are carried out within the work order, customer authorization, warranty and asset responsibility scope; for matters beyond authorization (such as non-original parts, modifications, unauthorized access), apply first and then act; document authorizations and exceptions.
Check six: do repair bills and inventory records match the actual actions

Repair bills and time cards and expense reports are completed according to the actual actions; parts requisition and inventory and ordering records match the actual replacements; repeat repairs and second visits are recorded separately with the reason, and the same fault is not masked with a new work order.

Computer, Automated Teller, and Office Machine Repairers repair, maintain or install computers, word processing systems, automated teller machines and office electronic equipment such as copiers and fax machines. The typical loop is to receive a work order and travel to the customer site or shop, confirm the symptoms with the customer, disassemble and test after isolation and safety confirmation to localize the fault, replace or adjust parts, reassemble and retest and calibrate to specifications, explain the repair result to the customer, and file the work order and bill and records; live electrical work and isolation and prevention of unexpected re-energization, access to and confidentiality of personal information on customer equipment, and warranty and asset and manufacturer authorization must be carried out by positions with the corresponding authority and qualifications, in accordance with the applicable jurisdiction and employer policies.

The exact identity on this page is O*NET-SOC49-2011.00, with tasks covering the repair, maintenance or installation of computers, ATMs and office electronic equipment. The interest indicators are RC (R81/C75/I28/E13/S13/A0), not a personal interest distribution or a hiring requirement. Job Zone1-2 and an SVP below 6.0 are the preparation level; the group's generic high school/GED statement is not the education survey distribution for this occupation.

Communication and customer contact｜94% have telephone conversations every day; 76% have face-to-face discussions every day (11% never); 87% use email every day (11% never); 63% consider dealing with external customers or the public extremely important (13% very important, 11% fairly important); 36% have sustained contact with others (19% contact about half the time).

Precision and pace｜57% consider repetitive tasks extremely important (23% not at all important); 35% consider being very exact or highly accurate extremely important (12% important, 11% fairly important); 64% face strict deadlines every day (12% at least once a week, 16% at least once a month); 14% write formal letters and memos every day (27% never); 81% work 40 hours per week (19% more than 40 hours); 82% have a regular fixed schedule (18% irregular).
Posture and physical work｜71% use their hands to handle objects and tools continuously or almost continuously (23% less than half the time); 40% stand continuously or almost continuously (26% more than half the time, 20% about half the time); 13% kneel, crouch or bend continuously or almost continuously (17% more than half the time); 13% bend or twist continuously or almost continuously (13% about half the time, 54% less than half the time); 46% need to walk or run less than half the time; 24% sit about half the time (40% never); 30% make repetitive motions less than half the time (20% never); 40% work somewhat close to others.
Site and environment｜70% work indoors in an environmentally controlled setting every day; 33% are in an enclosed vehicle or operating enclosed equipment every day (23% never); 22% are outdoors exposed to all weather conditions every day (62% never); 16% work in an uncontrolled indoor environment at least once a week; 78% never work outdoors under cover; 28% are exposed to contaminants every day (16% never); 22% are exposed daily to very hot or very cold temperatures (52% never); 12% are exposed to distracting noise at least once a week (22% at least once a month).
Hazards and protection｜18% are exposed to hazardous conditions every day (37% never); 22% are exposed every day to minor burns and cuts and bites or stings (32% never); 12% are exposed to hazardous equipment at least once a month (77% never); 12% are exposed to heights at least once a month (86% never); 86% never climb ladders or scaffolds; 22% wear common protective and safety equipment at least once a month (54% never); 91% never wear specialized protective and safety equipment; 98% never come into contact with radiation; 94% never come into contact with whole body vibration.
Automation and collaboration｜42% of the work is moderately automated (11% slight, 33% not at all automated); 11% consider the pace of work being determined by equipment speed extremely important (15% important, 65% not at all important); 21% consider work with a work group or team extremely important (16% important, 11% not at all important); 14% consider coordinating or leading others extremely important (26% important, 23% not at all important); 14% consider competition extremely intense (19% very intense, 27% not at all intense).
Conflict and pressure｜13% face conflict situations every day (42% at least once a week, 16% at least once a month, 19% never); 16% deal at least once a week with unpleasant or angry or discourteous people (29% at least once a year); 51% consider the consequences of error serious (15% fairly serious, 24% not at all serious); 34% need to keep or regain balance less than half the time (62% never).
Boundaries and authorization｜Live electrical work and isolation and prevention of unexpected re-energization, access to and confidentiality of personal information on customer equipment, and warranty and asset and manufacturer authorization must be carried out by positions with the corresponding authority and qualifications, in accordance with the applicable jurisdiction and employer policies; test data and replaced parts and customer authorization must be documented and reviewable; the U.S. wages on this page are BLS May 2025 data, and employment and the projection follow the BLS 2025—2035 scope; precise occupational pay for mainland China is still missing, and the related industry average for category 812 repair enterprises serves only as background and cannot be used to derive personal wages.

The six directions share some capabilities with this occupation: understanding equipment and drawings, troubleshooting by symptom, communicating with customers or colleagues, and recording process and results. The real difference lies in the object and the authorization: this occupation covers computers, ATMs and office electronic equipment and does component-level replacement; operator positions only use the equipment; the coin machine and audio-visual directions have different objects; the electrical and electronic installation direction involves electrical power work and construction permits; and support positions mainly handle software and networks and accounts and usually do not do hardware disassembly and repair. When choosing, it is advisable to first validate with one deliverable exercise in "symptoms — test sequence — replacement and retesting — work order records," rather than comparing titles first.

The comparison basis is the occupational definition and the 25 tasks and work activities and work context descriptions on the O*NET-SOC 49-2011.00 page, the related occupations and adjacent occupation codes listed on that page, the adjacent occupation slug list registered in this evidence route (office-machine-operators-except-computer, coin-vending-and-amusement-machine-servicers-and-repairers, audiovisual-equipment-installers-and-repairers, electrical-and-electronics-installers-and-repairers), and the public occupational materials for each adjacent occupation; the comparison is an editorial compilation and does not constitute electrical safety, data compliance or legal conclusions.

The table below compares the positions and occupations adjacent to this occupation: office machine operators (except computer), coin vending and machine servicers and repairers, equipment installers (audio-visual equipment installation and repair), electrical and electronic equipment installers and repairers, computer support specialists and computer network support specialists. The four columns each answer the same kind of question: what the direction does, where the key difference from this occupation lies, and what kind of person is better suited to choosing it.

Office machine operators (except computer) operate and tend equipment and complete routine work and are not responsible for disassembly and inspection and component-level repair; this occupation is responsible for restoring the equipment to a usable state.
People willing to operate equipment per procedure and ensure output suit that direction; people willing to physically disassemble and reassemble and troubleshoot faults suit this occupation.
Mainly operation records and output and quality records.
Office machine operators (except computer)

Coin vending and machine servicers and repairers serve coin-operated and amusement equipment, and the fault types and scope of authorization differ from office equipment; this occupation covers computers and ATMs and office electronic equipment.
People willing to maintain coin-operated equipment in public places suit that direction; people willing to handle computers and office equipment suit this occupation.
Mainly collection and restocking and coin machine maintenance records.
Coin vending and machine servicers and repairers

Equipment installers (audio-visual equipment installation and repair) mainly install and wire audio-visual equipment, usually involving rigging and cable routing; this occupation mainly does component-level repair inside equipment.
People willing to install and wire audio-visual equipment suit that direction; people willing to do component-level diagnosis and replacement suit this occupation.
Mainly installation and wiring and commissioning records.
Equipment installers (audio-visual equipment installation and repair)

Electrical and electronic equipment installers and repairers work on electrical and electronic systems at construction and industrial sites, usually involving electrical power work and construction permits; this occupation works at equipment level with manufacturer technical materials and warranty authorization as the boundary.
People willing to install and repair on-site electrical systems suit that direction; people willing to troubleshoot within equipment-level scope suit this occupation.
Mainly electrical installation and inspection and acceptance records.
Electrical and electronic equipment installers and repairers

Computer support specialists mainly provide remote or on-site support for software and accounts and desktop issues and usually do not do component-level disassembly and repair; this occupation mainly does hardware disassembly and inspection and parts replacement.
People willing to do software and account and desktop support suit that direction; people willing to do hardware disassembly and assembly and retesting suit this occupation.
Mainly work orders and configuration and account handling records.
Computer support specialists

Computer network support specialists mainly configure and troubleshoot network devices and servers, involving network and system authority; this occupation covers client devices and office electronic equipment.
People willing to troubleshoot networks and servers suit that direction; people willing to do on-site equipment repair suit this occupation.
Mainly network configuration and fault and change records.
Computer network support specialists

Moving from this occupation to an adjacent direction usually requires filling in new competencies and authorization: the operator direction requires equipment operation and output and quality record experience; the coin machine direction requires collection and on-site work and coin machine maintenance experience; the audio-visual installation direction requires wiring and rigging and commissioning experience; the electrical and electronic installation direction requires qualifications for electrical power work and construction and acceptance experience; the computer support direction requires operating system and account and desktop support experience; the network support direction requires network configuration and troubleshooting experience. Hands-on ability and testing approach can transfer, but the object and the authorization boundary of each direction must be rebuilt.

paragraphs: Boundary: the six risk cards below summarize this occupation's tasks and work context to explain "what you will encounter and how it can be controlled"; they do not state incidence rates or accident probabilities; the applicable scope of each measure must be confirmed separately under the applicable jurisdiction and employer policy and manufacturer requirements.

Direct answer: the risks this occupation most needs to judge in advance come from three places — electric shock and equipment damage from live work and electrical injury, privacy and compliance liability from viewing or retaining data on customer equipment, and equipment damage and billing disputes from misdiagnosis and repeat repairs; exceeding warranty and asset authorization, on-site travel and workstation load, and inconsistencies between parts and inventory and work order records will amplify these three types of risk.

Evidence scope: O*NET supports the U.S. occupational tasks and work context; OSHA publications support general safety principles for electrical hazard control; Articles 5, 6, 9, 13 and 14 of the Personal Information Protection Law support the boundaries of lawfulness, necessity, security and processing basis in mainland China. The six specific scenarios, consequences and verification actions are editorial compilations; accident rates, contract warranty and the specific safety procedures for particular models were not verified and must be confirmed with the employer or qualified personnel.
Positions responsible for live work and electrical checks

Disassembling and inspecting electrical parts without isolating per procedure or preventing unexpected re-energization may cause electric shock and secondary equipment damage and affect personal safety.

Editor's verification suggestion: before disassembly, confirm with qualified personnel the isolation, lockout and prevention of unexpected re-energization procedures, test instruments and protection requirements for the applicable model. OSHA publications provide only general principles, and this page did not obtain model-specific voltage verification, discharging or re-energization procedures; do not operate without training or authorization, and do not treat a diagnostic need as a live-work permit.
Not isolating to save time; checking only the switch position without verifying voltage; treating live measurement as routine; lacking personal protection and tool checks.
Positions that come into contact with customer equipment data

Viewing, copying or retaining customer personal information without a lawful processing basis or beyond the scope necessary for the repair may cause privacy and compliance risk and harm trust. Lawful and necessary processing must still follow purpose, scope and security requirements; business data is verified separately against the contract and confidentiality policy.

Editor's verification suggestion: contact data only within the lawful basis, the clearly defined purpose and the minimum necessary scope; before backing up or resetting, explain the scope and data risk to the customer and verify the lawful processing basis and authorization against the work order and organizational procedures. Article 13 of the Personal Information Protection Law provides several lawful bases, and Article 14 requires written consent only where the law requires it, so not all repairs should be written as requiring statutory written consent.
Casually browsing customer files or photos; connecting equipment to a personal account; leaving identifiable data on a personal computer or in external tools.
Positions responsible for warranty and asset and authorization judgments

Replacing parts or modifying beyond the work order and customer, asset or manufacturer authorization may cause contract and billing disputes; whether warranty is affected must be verified against the actual warranty terms, and it cannot be asserted unconditionally that non-original parts void the warranty.

Carry out the work within the work order and customer authorization and warranty and asset responsibility scope; for matters beyond authorization (non-original parts, modifications, unauthorized access), apply first and then act; document the authorization scope and exceptions and the customer's confirmation.
Replacing parts first and backfilling authorization later; filling in work outside the warranty scope on a warranty form; not recording modifications and broken seals.
Positions that carry on-site travel and physical and workstation load
Frequent travel and lifting equipment and long periods of standing and bending bring traffic accident risk and musculoskeletal and repetitive strain injuries.

Plan journeys according to dispatch routes and working hours and avoid driving while fatigued; use aids and correct posture when lifting and ask for help; adjust workstation and tool heights and change posture periodically; wear common protective equipment as required.
Driving while fatigued to meet response times; lifting heavy equipment alone; maintaining the same posture for long periods; omitting protective equipment.
Positions responsible for diagnosis and replacement decisions
Replacing parts directly from experience or handing over without completing retesting causes misrepairs and repeat service calls and equipment damage and affects the customer and billing.

Turn the customer's description into testable hypotheses and rule them out item by item with instrument or diagnostic software results; distinguish mechanical from electrical faults and avoid replacing parts first from experience; retest and calibrate to specifications and write the test data into the work order.
Reaching a conclusion when the symptom does not reproduce; not doing a control test; retesting only for "it powers on" without checking performance and stability.
Positions responsible for parts and inventory and work order billing
Parts requisition and inventory and ordering records that do not match the actual replacements cause cost and inventory distortion and affect warranty and billing and audit.

Register requisition and replacement and return according to the actual actions and retain the old parts or handling records; complete bills and time cards and expense reports according to the facts; record repeat repairs and second visits separately with the reason and do not mask the same fault with a new work order.

Replacing the part first and backfilling paperwork later; not investigating inventory discrepancies; masking repeat repairs with a new work order; expense reports that do not match the actual journey.

values: Fictitious task: based on a fictitious fault work order and a fictitious equipment manual, complete the symptom organization and test sequence and criteria and the replacement and retesting plan and the work order record.

Step one: write the symptoms and test sequence and criteria (turn the customer's description into testable hypotheses, and point out the place in the given materials where mechanical and electrical are hard to distinguish).

Step two: write the disassembly and inspection and replacement and retesting plan (list the isolation and voltage testing and disassembly and assembly sequence and part matching and retesting criteria, and explain how to prove the equipment is truly restored to working order after replacement).

Evaluation basis: whether the test sequence is executable, whether the mechanical and electrical judgment is justified, whether isolation and voltage testing and safety steps are complete, whether the retesting criteria are testable, whether the work order includes customer authorization and data handling, and whether judgments beyond authority are identified as requiring authorized confirmation.

entries.answer: Daily work is mainly on-site diagnosis and fault localization, parts replacement and retesting, and installation and configuration and customers and records: travel to customers' stores or offices to repair equipment or provide emergency repair service; talk with customers to establish the fault details and disassemble and test to localize the defect; use hand or power tools to repair, adjust or replace electrical or mechanical parts and reassemble; operate machines to test function and align, adjust and calibrate to specifications; install and configure new equipment and operating system software and peripherals; reinstall or adjust software settings; maintain parts inventory and order spare parts; explain operation and maintenance to customers; and maintain repair records and complete bills and time cards and expense reports. The page's work context shows 94% have telephone conversations every day, 76% have face-to-face discussions every day, 71% use their hands to handle objects and tools continuously or almost continuously, and 40% stand continuously or almost continuously.
entries.question: What do computer, automated teller and office machine repairers do every day?

entries.answer: Office machine operators (except computer) use the equipment and are not responsible for disassembly and inspection and component-level repair; coin vending and machine servicers serve coin-operated and amusement equipment, with a different object and authorization; equipment installers (audio-visual equipment installation and repair) mainly install and wire audio-visual equipment; electrical and electronic equipment installers and repairers work at construction and industrial sites, usually involving high voltage and construction permits; computer support specialists mainly support software and accounts and desktops and usually do not do hardware disassembly and repair; computer network support specialists mainly configure and troubleshoot networks and servers. This occupation centers on restoring computers, ATMs and office electronic equipment to a usable state and delivering the work order. Shared competencies do not mean interchangeability: the object and the authorization differ.
entries.question: Where is the boundary between this occupation and adjacent occupations?

entries.answer: It cannot be inferred that way. The core tasks of this occupation include on-site symptom judgment and disassembly and inspection, execution of live-work risk and safety procedures, parts replacement and retesting, and accountability for customer equipment data and work orders and billing; these steps depend on hands-on ability and safety authorization. In addition, the ILO exposure index registered in this evidence route is only a task exposure measure, not a replacement rate or a forecast of job losses. The more reliable use of tools is fault code classification and material retrieval and record drafts.
entries.question: Will AI replace this occupation?

entries.answer: From the task structure, the steps affected earlier are the structured and digitizable ones: fault code and error log classification, technical material and historical work order retrieval, generation of test steps and records and work order and expense drafts, and spare parts matching and inventory summaries. Affected later are the steps requiring hands-on work and responsibility: on-site symptom judgment and disassembly sequence, execution of live-work risk and safety procedures, assembly and calibration and retesting criteria, and customer data access and warranty and authorization judgments. It must be emphasized: this judgment is an editorial compilation, not an exposure measure or job forecast provided by the sources.
entries.question: Which tasks are most easily assisted?

entries.answer: Working out an executable test sequence by symptom and verifying it on the actual machine, working safely within the live and isolated boundaries, judging whether assembly and calibration and retesting truly meet the standard, and limiting data on customer equipment to the necessary scope and writing the work order clearly. These abilities depend on hands-on experience and safety authorization and professional habits; replacing any of these steps with tool output makes "whether the equipment is truly repaired and who is accountable for customer data and billing" unanswerable.

description.text: Computer, Automated Teller, and Office Machine Repairers repair, maintain or install computers and word processing systems and automated teller machines and office electronic equipment such as copiers and fax machines, centered on on-site diagnosis and fault localization, parts replacement and retesting, and installation and configuration and customers and records: the 25 tasks and work context, the U.S. BLS May 2025 median wage of 47,810 USD and the 2025—2035 employment change of -3.0%, the registered mainland China wage gap and the decision not to publish a figure, entry and qualification and authorization paths, and live work and data and warranty boundaries and the exercise are all laid out in one view.

subject.name: Computer, Automated Teller, and Office Machine Repairers
subject.summary: Repair, maintain or install computers, word processing systems, automated teller machines and office electronic equipment such as copiers and fax machines: travel to customers' stores or offices to repair equipment or provide emergency repair service; talk with customers to establish the fault details and disassemble machines to inspect parts for wear or defects; use oscilloscopes and multimeters or diagnostic software to test circuits to locate defects; use hand or power tools to repair, adjust or replace electrical or mechanical parts and reassemble; assemble, align, adjust and calibrate to specifications; operate machines to test function; install and configure new equipment and operating system software and peripherals; reinstall or adjust software settings; update existing equipment; maintain parts inventory and order spare parts; explain operation and maintenance to customers; and maintain repair records and complete bills and time cards and expense reports.
